page_title: REST Servers in Go: Part 4 - using OpenAPI and Swagger

summary.title: REST Servers in Go: Part 4 - using OpenAPI and Swagger
summary.one_liner: You learn how OpenAPI/Swagger can standardize REST API descriptions, what Go code generators can and cannot do for you, and why the author prefers generating specs from code over generating server code.
keywords: generate openapi spec from go code
how to describe a rest api
takeaways: OpenAPI (current name of the spec, formerly Swagger) gives REST APIs a standard, machine-readable description that serves as a contract and auto-generates documentation.
Code generated by swagger-codegen for Go was mostly a stub; the author had to restructure it, add parameter validation manually, and found it diverged from the spec quickly.
go-swagger supports only Swagger 2.0 and ties the server to its own opinionated framework and dependencies.
oapi-codegen produced simpler, cleaner Go code and accepts OpenAPI v3, though it pulls in a third-party dependency for parameter binding.
Generating an OpenAPI spec from annotated server code (swaggo/swag) is presented as a balanced alternative to generating the server from the spec.
summary.summary: The post is Part 4 of a series on writing REST servers in Go. It explains the history and naming of Swagger and OpenAPI, then rewrites the task service by hand-writing an OpenAPI 3.0 YAML spec in Swagger Editor. The author then evaluates code generators: swagger-codegen (official, mostly stub server), go-swagger (Swagger 2.0 only, opinionated framework), and oapi-codegen (clean code, OpenAPI v3, one extra dependency), and also covers generating specs from code annotations with swaggo/swag. The conclusion favors using OpenAPI for documentation and contracts while being cautious about generating the server code itself.
